method: The threads start from Amit's own account in episode 128 (the state, firms, Indian finance, the foundational episodes and the private passions), split and extended until every episode had a home, with each episode placed from its title, chapters, blurb and core ideas, and the insight files where those were not enough. Each path opens with the episodes the hosts themselves link back to most in their show notes, then moves to applications and finally to the newest or most contested episodes; every 'why' paraphrases that episode's own blurb, chapters or insights. Start-here picks are heavily linked foundations whose linked neighbours span many threads, plus episodes that show both hosts at full stretch.

start_here.why: The show's keystone, linked from 19 later episodes: freedom as consent, then India's economic history through that lens.
The base of the state thread, linked from 14 episodes: the state as violence, so every intervention carries moral cost.
Ajay makes finance make sense through its history; 15 later episodes on finance and firms build on it.
The development thesis in one sitting: failure is the norm, and success needs capable firms, a capable state, accountable politics.
A 101 masterclass: why trade is positive-sum and tariffs hurt your own poor; later globalisation episodes build on it.
Both hosts telling stories: India's quiet reformers pitched as a web series, and a lesson in how change happens.
The O-ring theory of why talent clusters, then Ajay on why new states fail; six later episodes build on it.
Amit's diabetes reversal doubles as a lesson in how a sugar lobby bent science; eight later episodes cite it.
Amit at his best with a poker presentation: expected value, variance and tilt, turned into lessons for life.
An intimate offering: the ten frameworks that shaped how the hosts see the world, from spontaneous order to giving unconditionally.

threads.name: Why freedom works: prices, consent and the unseen
threads.summary: Why do free people coordinating through prices outperform planners, and why do well-meant interventions so often hurt the poor? This thread builds the show's core toolkit (freedom as consent, prices as a knowledge machine, the seen and the unseen, the fallacies that fool us) and then tests it on population, vaccines, crime, speech, privacy and gig work.

path.why: The show's keystone: freedom as consent, a world that is not zero-sum, and spontaneous order over design.
The two lenses everything else uses: Bastiat's unseen costs and Hayek's prices as distributed knowledge.
Goes to the source texts: Hayek on prices, Coase on why firms exist, Friedman on monetary policy, Bastiat again.
Hazlitt's one lesson worked through public works, taxes, machinery and rent control, ending in a reusable toolkit.
Price caps, rent control, minimum wages, MSPs and tariffs: five meddlings with prices, one pattern of harm.
Five foundational fallacies, from zero-sum thinking to treating people as chess pieces, and how to spot them.
Why fashionable elite positions on socialism, inequality, victimless crimes and price controls end up hurting the poor.
Economic, social and political freedom come as one bundle: why the Soviet model broke and China's is breaking.
People are brains, not stomachs; population control shows coercion reaching for the body, its last frontier.
A hard case: the hosts love vaccines, yet argue that state coercion to vaccinate is mostly unjustified.
Alcohol, drugs, gambling, sex work: why criminalising acts that harm no one else breeds black markets.
Amit's case for free speech absolutism, the chilling effect, and why a weak state needs a higher bar.
Financial privacy is simply personal privacy: why India's KYC is the world's worst, and why we shouldn't normalise it.
Steelmans the critics, then argues gig work is freedom and consent in action: the urban NREGS.
Liberal, conservative, socialist, libertarian, nationalist: what the labels mean, and the first principles the hosts share.
The capstone: ten frameworks, from spontaneous order and distrust of the state to the double thank-you moment.

threads.name: How the state works, and fails
threads.summary: What is the state, when should it act, and why do well-meant interventions so often go wrong? Starting from the state as organised coercion and public choice's view of politicians and bureaucrats as people responding to incentives, the thread builds a test for intervention and applies it to vaccines, regulators, digital public infrastructure, industrial policy, the military and research funding.

path.why: First principles: the state's existence is itself violence, so every intervention carries a moral cost; scope versus strength.
Freedom as the default, the four market failures, least-intrusive tools, and why state capability takes generations.
Politics without romance: politicians, bureaucrats, lobbies and voters all respond to incentives, so government failure is ubiquitous.
The first case study: using the previous two episodes' toolkit to ask when vaccine coercion could be justified.
Ajay on why new states mostly fail: coercive power without cladding, and institutions that take years to build.
Why running a country like a company fails: different feedback loops, a guaranteed monopoly, coercion, rules versus deals.
Why policies transplanted from abroad fail: the invisible infrastructure of incentives and checks they silently depend on.
Applies high modernism and premature legibility to UPI and Aadhaar: what a state monopoly does to competition.
How Indian regulators came to fuse legislative, executive and judicial power, and what the FSLRC proposed instead.
Necessary is not enough: a four-metric test of how hard an intervention is, from monetary policy to financial regulation.
Scott's legibility, high modernism and metis, with Prussian forestry and Mao's sparrows as warnings against grand schemes.
Picking winners through subsidies and PLI: why industrial policy is born of hubris and redistributes from poor to rich.
The state toolkit applied to defence: threats first, foundational processes, and why self-reliant procurement fails.
The frontier: Amit and Ajay disagree on whether the state should fund innovation, then agree on contracting it out.

threads.name: Keeping power in check: rules, democracy and populism
threads.summary: What stops those who hold power from abusing it, and what wears those restraints down? The thread first lays out the machinery of a free republic (rules over discretion, separation of powers, decentralisation, legitimacy), then examines the forces that erode it: populism, nationalism, the law used as harassment, curbs on speech, a captured media and the lure of crisis.

path.why: Strong rules, not strong rulers: credible commitment beats the strongman, from monetary policy to parenting.
Democracy as dispersed power: separating the planner from the doer, and where India's regulators and anti-defection law go wrong.
Dispersing power vertically: why diverse India needs empowered cities, more states and the subsidiarity principle.
Weber's sources of legitimacy and what decays without it, then Amit's counter: compliance is not consent.
Populism defined precisely, as 'only some of the people are the people', with its playbook traced through four countries.
Amit's case that nationalism lets the state become the ruler, and essentialises, then dehumanises, people.
When rulers control indictment, the process becomes the punishment: a layered design for investigation and prosecution.
Free speech as the check on power: the chilling effect, process as punishment, and Indian elites' hypocrisy.
Eight crises of the Indian media, from money and trust to the state's stick and carrot.
Why crises usually end badly, through malice or incompetence, instead of opening the door to reform.
Havel, Nehru, Manmohan Singh, Zelenskyy, Carney: what outsiders bring to power, and how the repeated game corrupts career politicians.

threads.name: How reform actually happens
threads.summary: If good ideas are known, why are they so rarely adopted, and how did India's real reforms get done? The thread follows Ajay's policy pipeline and the long game played by India's quiet reformers, then walks through reforms that stuck, decayed or were botched (farm policy, pensions, inflation targeting, bankruptcy, financial regulation, GST), ending with the myth that crises make reform easy.

path.why: The silent freedom movement: the economists and bureaucrats who quietly reformed India after 1947, pitched as a web series.
Ajay's policy pipeline, the Overton window, and why society changes ten percent at a time.
How a past generation's expert consensus built India's farm controls, and how farmer leaders like Sharad Joshi spoke Hayek.
A full reform cycle: the old pension scheme's crisis, the NPS consensus, and how reform decays without an ecosystem.
An insider's account of a reform that worked, and why reform moves at the speed of the intellectual climate.
The bankruptcy code: an excellent design in a C-grade environment, and why reform needs a knowledge ecosystem.
The FSLRC story, and Ajay's claim that the theory of change is persuasion and research communities, not cathedrals.
From the 2004 GST proposal Ajay co-wrote to a flawed implementation, and why change starts upstream of policymakers.
The frontier: why waiting for a crisis is a bad theory of change, and incrementalism usually wins.

threads.name: Firms: where prosperity is made
threads.summary: Why are rich countries rich? This thread's answer is firms: how they are owned and governed, how they grow, go global and die, how the state helps or hobbles them, and what it takes to start one. Amit says the centrality of firms was the idea he had not fully internalised before EIE.

path.why: Four designs from owner-deity to modern board, and why a rich country is made of sophisticated firms.
Coase's 'Nature of the Firm': why firms exist at all, and joining one as a voluntary contract.
What development economics missed: firms are the site where GDP is made, so leave them firms alone.
Indian firms went from local satraps to national homogenisers; now they must adapt to a hundred different Indias.
Sun, Google and Amazon: leaps of imagination that came from storytelling, not linear business logic.
Firm productivity decides prosperity: six modes of internationalisation, and why success at home is bad training.
Foreign firms as carriers of knowledge and better institutions, and why India has so often fought them.
Creative destruction needs death as well as birth: how bankruptcy frees people and capital from zombie firms.
What the state does to firms when it picks winners, and why enabling winners beats picking them.
Twelve reasons manufacturing doesn't work in India today, from minimum wages to stepped regulation that keeps firms micro.
Gig platforms as a Coasean milestone: the algorithm replaces the manager and the firm's boundary shrinks.
Your turn: why to start a business, and the mindset it takes: love over like, internal drive, bias for action.
Thirteen founder principles: be a generalist, serve the customer, optimise for truth-telling, keep an inner scorecard.

threads.name: Indian finance, the brain of the economy
threads.summary: Finance looks forbidding from outside, yet it is how an economy decides which firms get capital and which must die. The thread opens with a guided history of finance, maps India's whole financial system, goes deep on inflation targeting, the exchange rate, bankruptcy, pensions and KYC, and ends with your own retirement and the unresolved fight over financial crises.

path.why: Ajay's guided history, from primitive times to derivatives, plus Timur Kuran on why the Middle East fell behind.
The map of India's whole financial system: banks, markets, currency controls, bankruptcy, monetary policy, surveillance, systemic risk.
Why inflation is a tax on the poor, and how inflation targeting gave the central bank a single job.
The exchange rate as the most important price: why 'strong' and 'weak' rupees mean nothing and floating stabilises.
Bankruptcy as a melting ice cube: how India's code works in practice, from creditors' committees to promoters.
Why defined-benefit pensions blow up, how the NPS was built, and why the fight has reopened.
Finance as a surveillance tool: the history of KYC, and why Aadhaar didn't fix India's version.
Personal finance done right: why there is no magic retirement number, and why global diversification matters most.
The frontier: why crises happen and what to do, with Amit's Austrian dissent from the conventional view.

threads.name: Why India is poor, and how it gets rich
threads.summary: Why is India still poor decades after Independence, and what would make it rich? The thread starts with India's economic history read as a story of freedom and the hosts' critique of development economics, goes sector by sector (population, farms, tourism, infrastructure, electricity, manufacturing, taxes), and ends with a roadmap for a hostile world and the show's final diagnosis.

path.why: India's economic history from before Independence to today, read as freedoms gained, lost and partly regained.
Why development economics failed poor countries: the 10x gap, failure as the norm, and Ajay's three pillars of development.
Population as India's greatest asset: density drives prosperity, and blamed 'population problems' are governance problems.
How land rules, APMC monopsonies and MSPs hobble farmers, and why development means moving people off farms.
A worked example: how Himalayan states could build sustainable tourism that benefits local people, not tourist traps.
Infrastructure powered India's services boom but not goods exports; why big projects stopped giving bang for buck.
The power sector's old world, the renewables opportunity, and why prices solve intermittency.
Nuclear as the safest energy, small modular reactors, and five conditions for India: an argument for freedom, not action.
The grim numbers on Indian manufacturing, and Amit's history of the Nehru- and Indira-era mistakes behind them.
Why the state shouldn't pick winning sectors either: modern manufacturing is high-skill, and services are now more tradable.
GDP first, tax-to-GDP second: how cascading taxes and blocked credits undercut a GST that was conceptually superb.
A roadmap after the US turned hostile: deep trade agreements, resilience over autarky, and reform at home.
The show's closing diagnosis: India's poverty lies upstream of the growth formula, in finance, firms and institutions.

threads.name: Trade, war and India's place in the world
threads.summary: Nations deal with one another through trade or through war, and the show argues that the first is a positive-sum alternative to the second. The thread starts with why globalisation is great and how it rose and receded, follows the US-China tech war and the return of tariffs, then turns to how wars are fought now, from Ukraine and insurgencies to drones and hybrid warfare.

path.why: The 101: trade is positive-sum, imports are the privilege, and tariffs move wealth from your poor to your rich.
Ajay's frame of three globalisations, the third shaped by economic statecraft, plus why trade deficits don't matter.
The gravity model and the cost of borders: South Asia's missing trade is missing welfare.
Globalisation of culture: salmon sushi isn't Japanese, most Indian food isn't Indian, and culture is a khichdi.
GATT's rise and stall, the Trumpist arguments taken seriously, and India's once-in-a-generation opportunity.
The Soviet backdrop and China's decades: why prosperity directed from above breaks, and what to learn from it.
The US-China tech war: export controls, why engagement collapsed, and the hosts split on economic warfare.
India's strategy as the US goes rogue: overinvest in the rule-bound two-thirds of advanced-economy trade.
Why the Ukraine war matters from India, and how battlefield transparency killed the breakthrough.
Fighting your own citizens: counterinsurgency is 20% military, 80% political, and India keeps getting it wrong.
Is India's military ready? Threats first, cost-efficient force design, and one notch behind the frontier plus scale.
Acts of war that don't look like war: detection, attribution and response, and epistemic institutions as the defence.
Drones, a 30-km hellscape and eight principles: why surprise and mass are dead and all roads lead to scale.
The frontier: satellite night lights reveal what war and sanctions are doing to Russia's economy.

threads.name: How knowledge is made, taught and measured
threads.summary: How does a society produce, spread and test knowledge, and why do India's universities, schools and exams do it so badly? The thread starts with the knowledge society and education, moves to the crafts of reading, writing papers and statistics, examines how knowledge is corrupted, resisted or lost, and ends with new data, from night lights to search bars, that lets us see the world afresh.

path.why: The three pillars of a knowledge society, why the academy became a circlejerk, and how creators can bypass gatekeepers.
Why more spending won't fix Indian education: fund schooling not schools, early childhood, and learning how to learn.
Exams as statistical estimators, the meritocracy lie, and Ajay's fixes, including free colleges and a lottery.
How to actually learn from books: building the habit, Adler's levels of reading, and Amit's note-taking workflow.
Question, answer, novelty: Ajay's masterclass on writing research, which doubles as a guide to clearer thinking.
What economists can learn from anthropologists and sociologists: cognitive empathy, taking words seriously, and studying process.
Statistics through stories: CR Rao, Abraham Wald's survivorship bias, and why random sampling beats a census.
How a cherry-picked study and a powerful sugar lobby built decades of wrong nutrition consensus.
Why the knowledge machine punishes people ahead of their time and selects only for conscientiousness.
Silphium, Dhaka muslin, Fogbank: tacit knowledge vanishes when people stop practising it, and institutions beat stones.
Measuring what official data hides: night lights from satellites as a proxy for economic activity.
New data on old questions: ancient genes show humanity is a khichri, and phone exhaust reveals behaviour.
Search bars and dating apps as polygraphs: the gap between what people say and what they reveal.

threads.name: Where progress comes from: talent, heretics and technology
threads.summary: Is progress made by lone geniuses, by clusters of talent, by heretics who defy consensus, or by relentless technological curves? The thread starts with Newton, Gandhi and why talent clusters, follows mavericks and outlaws whose ideas were resisted, then turns to technologies (Unix, Moore's laws, maps, AI) and the state's role in innovation, ending with predictions for 2050.

path.why: Is genius a product of historical forces or an accident? Newton and Gandhi as the two test cases.
The O-ring theory: why talent needs the right place and people, from Silicon Valley to Bollywood.
Oppenheimer's story: maverick mode versus bureaucracy mode, and the tragedy of the Oppenheimers who never were.
CR Rao as the Bengal Renaissance's finest product, and why eccentric founders like Mahalanobis beat bureaucracies.
Semmelweis, Wegener, Wollstonecraft and more: pathbreakers reviled in their lifetimes by the aggressively conventional.
Heretics who rethought fundamentals, from angioplasty's pioneers to Sri Lankan cricket, prompted by Amit's own heart attack.
Bell Labs as a special place and moment, and the Unix philosophy of small tools that became technology's backbone.
Moore's, Wright's and Goddard's laws: the price curves behind recent progress, and learning by doing.
From George Everest's surveys to GPS and satellites: how maps took us from darkness to light.
Can the state amplify innovation? Spillovers, NASA, NIH and NMITLI, and a proposal to contract research out.
Mixtapes, letters, STD booths, cash: progress is good, yet some lost objects held ways of living worth keeping.
AI as a tool for a master: Amit defends it, Ajay attacks LLMs, and neither fears the paperclip maximiser.
Fifteen humble predictions for 2050, from AI-generated entertainment and gene editing to lab-grown meat.

threads.name: Know thyself: evolution, sex, faith and culture
threads.summary: What are humans like beneath politics and policy? This thread takes evolution as the master frame (biology as hardware, culture as software) and applies it to desire, ancestry, culture, religion and the changing ways men and women find each other, ending with how technology may remake relationships by 2050.

path.why: The show's first episode plants the frame: biology is hardware, culture is software we can upgrade.
Natural and sexual selection, epigenetics and the is-ought trap: why understanding evolution is how to know yourself.
Evolution applied to desire: visual versus narrative cues, the asymmetry of reproductive cost, and why hardwiring isn't destiny.
What searches and dating apps reveal about men and women: the Tinder Gini, the sex recession, marriage unbundled.
Ancient DNA as a record of who we are: humanity is a khichri, and caste endogamy can be dated.
Culture as software in action: food, clothes and language keep mixing, so 'cultural appropriation' is incoherent.
Hinduism as a river, not a book: open-source epics, colonial othering and the rise of Hindutva.
Atheism as an absence of belief, the four functions of religion, and morality built from hardware, norms and reason.
Rapid-fire verdicts on human questions: hardware versus trainable software, marriage unbundled, lust versus love, solitude.
The frontier: remapped relationships, gene editing and reproduction inside machines by 2050.

threads.name: Stories, form and the creative life
threads.summary: How are great stories and creative works made, and how is the creator's life changing? The thread starts with the hosts' pitches for stories that should be films and the seven basic plots, moves through artists from Springsteen to the Spanish masters, and ends with form, constraint and the creator economy, including the lessons of making EIE itself.

path.why: The film-pitch series begins: seven stories, from a nonviolent warrior tribe to WW2's fat frogs and a child widow.
Why stories work: Booker's seven basic plots, from Jaws to Sholay, and structure as trampoline, not cage.
Five more pitches, each zooming from the fate of the world to one person facing one problem.
Pitching India's quiet reformers as a web series: form versus spectacle, and a recurring image as narrative spine.
Fiction built from IIT aspirants and vloggers, plus true tales of missing plutonium and 1800s Delhi.
The last pitches, with craft notes: Chekhov's gun, show-don't-tell, and two models of filmmaking.
Springsteen's songs as literature: write what's around you, make the specific universal, refuse to cover yourself.
Velázquez, Goya, Picasso and Miró did their most powerful work in old age: audiences freeze artists, masters keep moving.
Amit's podcasting masterclass: why audio is intimate, the art of conversation, and lessons for any creator.
Form is born of constraint: why songs, albums and books take their shapes, and why creators can now break them.
Joni Mitchell, Frida Kahlo, Dr Seuss, Fosbury: pioneers who broke new ground because of their constraints.
The show's own creator lessons: bias for action, stock versus flow, loved by a few, ignore analytics for two years.

threads.name: Private passions: what the hosts love for its own sake
threads.summary: Alongside the public-purpose threads, EIE made room for what the hosts love for its own sake: poker, cricket, chess, cycling, hiking, Unix, maps, music, painting and reading. Each episode is a joy on its own terms, and each smuggles in a way of thinking, from expected value and process over outcome to knowing when to turn back.

path.why: Amit's poker presentation: expected value, variance and tilt, then what the game teaches about luck and peace.
Poker's expected value applied to cricket, and why T20 demands aggression.
The world championship from 1886 to Gukesh, how computers changed chess, and why it is still a human game.
Chess in 2024 as life lessons: Gukesh and Arjun's different journeys, Magnus's misbehaviour, mastery versus renewal.
Why cycling is a team sport of slipstreams, domestiques and breakaways, plus its drug-era drama.
Ajay's lifelong love of hiking: how to start, knowing when to turn back, and character under stress.
Ajay's other love: the history and philosophy of Unix, with a screencast teaching you to use it.
Ajay's childhood passion for maps: India's map history, today's map paradise, and an exam Amit sets him.
What Springsteen's music means to Ajay personally, and the aspects of his work Amit admires.
Amit's art education on a Spanish vacation, introducing four masters and their late work.
A personal one: the thought process that made Amit a non-believer, with common myths about atheism busted.
The passion both hosts share most: why read, how to build the habit, and how to read a book.

threads.name: The art of living: habits, choices and the long game
threads.summary: How should you work, decide and spend your days? This thread gathers the hosts' practical philosophy (staying open to changing your mind, escaping a single version of yourself, habits, thinking in expected value, health, decluttering, serendipity, starting a business) and ends with the frameworks that shaped them.

path.why: Be an anti-uncle: stay open to changing your mind, and know the four quadrants of conformism.
How small accidents harden into identity, and why self-awareness is the only escape from social programming.
Amit's productivity toolkit (just do it, habits, a second brain) and Ajay on quality and purpose.
Judge decisions by expected value, not results, and treat your career as your biggest undiversifiable bet.
Amit's diabetes reversal: a glucose monitor, eating order, fasting, and changing your food tribe.
Things you own end up owning you: decluttering stuff, preoccupations and toxic people, and saying no.
Excellence times exposure: why putting yourself out there makes you luckier, and why there are no strangers.
Why everyone should try starting a business: the owner's gaze, love over like, and bias for action.
Founder habits that are life habits: first principles, truth-telling, simplicity, professional pride, an inner scorecard.
Good gyan from Twitter on perception, happiness, courage and purpose, with Ajay's own additions.
More good gyan: thick versus thin desires, passion projects, imperfectionism, and why there is no 'making it'.
Rapid verdicts on life: travel versus tourism, happiness as hindsight, frugality that buys freedom, and lively disagreements.
The episode-50 AMA: parenting, reading lists, habits, meaning, and what the hosts would denormalise.
The episode-100 AMA: self-reflection as compounding, time as the real scarcity, communities of choice.
The capstone: ten frameworks that shaped the hosts, from 'play to play' to 'give unconditionally'.
